Here’s what we know right now.
 Print this Article 
 View Comments As of now, the best chance for snow sits across the interior late in the week. A modest nor'easter holds a decent chance of bringing a coating to 2 inches of snow in a few higher-elevation spots across Western Mass., and Northern New England (Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine). Boston Globe You may have noticed some chatter about snow being forecast for New England later in the week. I think it’s fair that you might be wondering if Boston and New England are about to get their first taste of winter and accumulating snow this season, at least away from the highest mountains. 
 Yes, some early signals show a coastal storm , a potential nor’easter, likely developing late week; I’d say sometime around Thursday and lasting through at least Friday. 
 And yes, I think we might see some accumulating snow (at least 1 inch) in spots across New England on Friday. 
 But I don’t believe a widespread and significant storm will impact our region, and Boston will not see any snow. The region should only see light to steady rain. 
 Right now, I think this modest storm holds a decent chance of bringing a coating to 2 inches in a few higher-elevation spots across Western Massachusetts and Northern New England. It just won’t be that cold around New England for widespread snow — Greater Boston may wind up with about an inch of rain, less than what we saw last week. 
 We might see some flakes mixing in at low elevations at times, but the odds of anything sticking, like across I-95 and I-495, are very low. 
 A coastal storm and potential nor'easter may arrive late Thursday through at least Friday, producing some snow at times across the interior. Boston Globe The forecast picture is nowhere near set on the storm’s track and strength, and my thoughts may very well change as the week progresses. But I just don’t think it will be a major storm. 
 But there is a lot of hype out there online right now and I want to discuss some details and what the models are showing right now. 
 The jet stream paints the picture — storms often develop on the eastern side of a U-shaped dip, or trough, in the jet stream. That’s because winds aloft in that area are fastest and spreading apart, creating what we call upper-level divergence. 
 As air spreads out high in the atmosphere, that triggers air near the surface to rapidly rise to fill the void, creating an area of low pressure. Those fast winds also allow the low to intensify while following along the jet stream “highway.” 
 A deep southerly bow in the jet stream should prompt a coastal low by Thursday, and moving near New England by sometime on Friday. Boston Globe 
 What the GFS model is showing
 The GFS model (the Global Forecast System or American model) takes the storm on a more inland track, which would favor rain for much of New England. However, colder air could allow snow to develop in the higher elevations, particularly across the mountains, from late Thursday into Saturday afternoon. 
 Closer to the coast, including Boston, there could be a few snowflakes spotted mixing in with periods of light rain. 
 The GFS suggests an interior track, with rain for most and upper-elevation snow from late Thursday through Saturday afternoon. Pivotal Weather What the European model is showing
 The European model (ECMWF or European Centre for Medium-Range Weather forecasts) takes the storm farther offshore, giving it more of a classic nor’easter track — but still a bit farther east to avoid big impacts. That would bring a better opportunity for snow in parts of interior New England, but even this scenario favors more rain than snow overall. 
 Once again, any accumulating snow would likely be scattered and focused across higher elevations. 
 The Euro model shows a track further out to sea, fitting the nor'easter profile, but still with more rain than snow. Snow is more scattered and in the higher elevations. Pivotal Weather 
 Forecast snow totals are all over the map
 The trend here is that snow totals are held to the interior. Between the NWS Blend of Models, the European and Euro-AI models, and the GFS, there is a wide range of what snow totals may look like. 
 Spotty coatings to 2 inches are more than likely, but the GFS and Euro-AI models show a couple of pockets of 2 to 4 inches in the higher elevations across Northern and Western New England. 
 Here are four forecast snowfall totals from the NWS Blend of Models, GFS, European, and Euro AI that show a wide range of snowfall later this week. Pivotal Weather So which model is more reliable? Dave Epstein, the Globe’s contributing meteorologist, typically leans toward the Euro, noting “it’s not always 100 percent right, but generally, you want to stick with what’s going to be mostly right.” 
 This chart shows five different weather forecasting models and how they compare. Dave Epstein Boston typically sees its first inch of snow around Dec. 11, and I suspect we’ll still be waiting for that 1 inch of snowfall after this storm passes. 
 This storm is obviously worth watching and requires continuous forecasting. But for now, I’d call this a modest fall storm and not a blockbuster nor’easter. 
 Boston stays with light rain, with maybe a snowflake sighting or two, but anything that accumulates would be well away from the city, across higher elevations of Western Mass. and Northern New England.
